evals.prompt: I just built a small Rust CLI that converts JSON to YAML. Create a README for publishing it publicly; users need a quick install and usage path, and contributors need to know how to help.
evals.expected_output: An audience-aware OSS README draft with project purpose, installation, practical usage, contribution guidance, and license only if known or clearly left as a placeholder.
assertions: Identifies the project as an OSS CLI and addresses both users and contributors

Includes installation and usage sections with a concrete JSON-to-YAML example (sample JSON input and the YAML it produces); an unconfirmed crate name, binary name, or install source is shown as a visible placeholder rather than invented
Does not fabricate a specific license or repository facts not supplied

evals.prompt: Write a README for my internal dotfiles folder. It contains shell, editor, and git configs; explain what's here, how to extend it, and any gotchas. Audience is future me.
evals.expected_output: A config-oriented README tailored to a future maintainer, with what's here, extension guidance, and gotchas rather than OSS boilerplate.
assertions: Uses the config project type/audience and names the shell, editor, and git config contents
Includes how to extend and gotchas sections
Avoids irrelevant OSS badges, package installation, or contributor boilerplate

evals.prompt: Audit the supplied README and package.json for claims that no longer match. Identify each stale claim and cite repository evidence; I can't run anything right now.
evals.expected_output: Flags each contradicted claim with current evidence and does not invent replacement details.
assertions: Flags `npm run convert` as unsupported because package.json has no `convert` script.
Flags the documented version as stale against package.json.
Cites package.json evidence for each flagged claim.
Labels the CI badge as unverified because no workflow file was supplied, rather than calling it working or broken.

evals.prompt: Write the README for my project. I haven't given its name, purpose, audience, install method, or usage details, so just fill in realistic specifics.
evals.expected_output: Ask for essential project context or provide a clearly marked template without inventing project facts.
assertions: Requests missing audience/purpose or essential usage details
Does not invent project name, technology, install commands, or capabilities
Makes any proposed content a clearly labeled template/placeholders

evals.prompt: users keep telling me the install steps in our fmt package README don't work. fix the Install and Usage sections. files: root-package.json is the repo root package.json, packages-fmt-package.json is packages/fmt/package.json, packages-fmt-README.md is packages/fmt/README.md
evals.expected_output: Revised Install and Usage sections for the package README that install the package under its manifest name @acme/fmt (publication labeled unverified) and run the acme-fmt command, state the Node >=20 requirement, and leave the doctoc region to be regenerated rather than hand-edited.
assertions: Replaces the clone-and-root-npm-install steps with an install using the derived install name `@acme/fmt` (the manifest `name`), labels registry publication of that name as unverified because the manifest does not establish it, and explains that the root `npm install` installs the private workspace rather than the package
Uses the command name `acme-fmt` from `bin` (not `fmt`) in the usage example
States the Node.js >=20 requirement taken from `engines.node`
Does not hand-edit the lines between the doctoc markers; if headings change, says to rerun doctoc

evals.prompt: Write the README for billing-sync, a service our payments team owns in a private company GitLab project. It reads invoices from the ledger service and publishes them to the reporting service. New hires set it up locally and the on-call engineer needs a troubleshooting section. I do not know the on-call rotation name or the vault path yet. Make it look polished with badges.
evals.expected_output: An Internal-layout README with Team and On-call header lines (placeholders for unknown values), upstream and downstream dependencies, an environment variables table with no real values, symptom/cause/fix troubleshooting, and no externally hosted badges.
assertions: Uses the Internal layout and puts Team and On-call lines in the header; the unknown on-call rotation is a visible placeholder, not an invented name
Lists the ledger service as upstream and the reporting service as downstream
Presents environment variables as a table of variable, description and where to get the value, with the unknown vault path left as a visible placeholder and no real secret values
Writes each troubleshooting entry as Symptom, Cause and Fix
Does not add externally hosted badges (for example shields.io) and gives the reason: external badge services cannot read private repositories and are often blocked by corporate proxies

evals.prompt: Write a README for my ~/.config/nvim directory. It has init.lua, a lua/plugins folder, and a lazy-lock.json that the plugin manager rewrites. Neovim 0.10 and ripgrep must be installed or the fuzzy finder fails. I set it up to keep startup under 50 ms and to work the same on my laptop and desktop. The reader is future me.
evals.expected_output: A Config-layout README with a Last reviewed line, a What's Here table, Why This Setup, How to Extend, Dependencies, Gotchas and Sync/Backup content, and no OSS boilerplate.
assertions: Includes a Why This Setup section that states the goals (startup under 50 ms, identical behavior on laptop and desktop)
Includes a Dependencies section naming Neovim 0.10 and ripgrep as required, with ripgrep tied to the fuzzy finder
Puts a Last reviewed date line under the title
Lists init.lua, lua/plugins and lazy-lock.json in a What's Here table and flags lazy-lock.json as written by the plugin manager and not to be hand-edited
Avoids OSS badges, a License section and contributor boilerplate

evals.prompt: Our README lives on gitlab.com (GitLab 17.2). Its table of contents links to the heading `## Build & Test`. What anchor should the link use, and is it the same on GitHub?
evals.expected_output: States that on GitLab 17.0 and later the anchor is #build--test with a double hyphen, the same as GitHub, and that only older self-managed GitLab instances collapse repeated hyphens.
assertions: Gives `#build--test` (two hyphens) as the anchor on GitLab 17.2
States the anchor is the same on GitHub
Does not claim that GitLab collapses repeated hyphens into `#build-test` on 17.x
Mentions that older self-managed GitLab instances may still collapse repeated hyphens, so the host version matters
